title: K-Concatenation Maximum Sum
description: Brute force to optimized: building and scanning the full repeated array versus Kadane's on 2 copies plus a closed-form adjustment for extra copies.

blocks.text: Given an integer array arr and an integer k, imagine arr repeated k times to form a much longer array. Return the maximum possible subarray sum of this repeated array, modulo 10^9 + 7. If the best possible sum would be negative, return 0 instead.

blocks.caption: Kadane's on just 2 copies of arr, plus extra full copies added only when helpful

blocks.text: Given arr and k, find the maximum subarray sum achievable in the array formed by repeating arr k times, without physically constructing that (potentially huge) array, returning the result modulo 10^9 + 7 (or 0 if negative).

blocks.title: Analogy: Sampling a Repeating Wallpaper Pattern
blocks.text: Like having a repeating wallpaper pattern and wanting to know the brightest possible contiguous strip achievable if the pattern repeated k times across a very long wall. Since the pattern repeats identically, any interesting strip either fits within roughly 2 repetitions of the base pattern (capturing any wrap-around effect at a seam) or benefits from including several more FULL repetitions of the pattern in between, but only if a full repetition's own total brightness is positive.

blocks.caption: 2 copies capture wrap-around shapes; extra full copies only help when the whole array sums positive

blocks.text: When every element of arr is negative, the best possible subarray sum is itself negative (or, treating the empty subarray as a valid zero-sum baseline, exactly 0). Since the problem specifies returning 0 rather than a negative result, initializing Kadane's running/best values to 0 (instead of the standard nums[0]) naturally produces the correct floor.
Before ever considering constructing the full k-times-repeated array, notice that any interesting subarray shape can be captured using just a small, fixed number of copies of arr.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A subarray of the repeated array either stays entirely within roughly one-and-a-bit copies of arr (possibly wrapping across a single seam between two copies), or it spans several FULL copies of arr in the middle, plus partial copies at each end.

Observation 2: Any wrap-around shape is already fully captured by running standard Kadane's Algorithm on just 2 concatenated copies of arr, since 2 copies contain every possible "wraps across one seam" subarray shape.

Observation 3: If arr's total sum is positive, including MORE full copies in the middle of a long subarray can only help (each additional full copy adds a positive amount); if totalSum is zero or negative, extra full copies never help and should be excluded entirely.

Observation 4: So the final answer is: run Kadane's on 2 copies of arr, and if k > 2 and totalSum > 0, add (k - 2) * totalSum to account for every additional full copy beyond the first two.

Recognizing that only 2 physical copies are ever needed (with any additional benefit expressible as a simple multiplication) is what avoids ever constructing the actual, potentially enormous, k-times-repeated array.

This reuses standard Kadane's Algorithm directly on a small, doubled array, combined with a simple arithmetic adjustment for any additional full copies, entirely avoiding the need to construct or scan the true k-times-repeated array.
Literally construct the full k-times-repeated array, then run standard Kadane's-style scanning directly over it.

For every possible starting index in this (potentially enormous) array, extend forward and track the maximum running sum.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The full array is constructed explicitly using modulo indexing into arr, since this brute force does not yet exploit the repeating structure.
best is initialized to 0, allowing the empty subarray as a valid baseline, matching this problem's specific requirement to return 0 rather than a negative result.

The final modulo operation is applied only once, at the very end, since intermediate sums here stay small enough not to require it during accumulation (though for very large k, care must be taken; the optimized solution below applies modulo only after the closed-form multiplication, avoiding this issue entirely by never summing k full copies directly).

blocks.text: Every possible subarray of the fully constructed repeated array is checked directly, so the correct maximum is always found, at the cost of actually building and scanning an enormous array.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((n * k) squared) in the worst case, since the repeated array has length n * k, and a full double loop scans it.
Space: O(n * k) to store the fully constructed repeated array, which can be prohibitively large.

Limitation: physically constructing and scanning the full repeated array ignores that any interesting subarray shape is already captured using just 2 copies of arr, with any further benefit expressible as a simple closed-form multiplication.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force builds and scans the entire k-times-repeated array. Instead, run standard Kadane's Algorithm on just 2 concatenated copies of arr (capturing every possible wrap-around subarray shape), initializing both the running and best values to 0 so the empty subarray serves as a valid zero-sum floor. Then, since additional full copies beyond the first two only ever help when arr's total sum is positive, add (k - 2) * totalSum to the 2-copy result exactly when that condition holds. Finally, apply the modulo operation to the result.

Compute totalSum of arr. Build doubled as 2 concatenated copies of arr (or just arr itself if k == 1). Run Kadane's Algorithm on doubled, with both running and best values starting at 0. If k > 2 and totalSum > 0, add (k - 2) * totalSum to the result. Return the result modulo 10^9 + 7.
Run Kadane's Algorithm on just 2 copies of arr, then add extra full copies' contribution only when it helps.
Dry run for arr = [1,-2,1], k = 5 (totalSum = 0, doubled = [1,-2,1,1,-2,1])

blocks.title: Combining the result
blocks.text: Kadane's on 2 copies gives best = 2. Since totalSum = 0 is not strictly positive, no extra copies contribute (0 * (k-2) = 0 regardless of k). Final answer: 2, matching the expected output.

codes.python:
def k_concatenation_max_sum(arr, k):
    MOD = 10**9 + 7

    def kadane_max(nums):
        best = 0                                                            # starting at 0 (not nums[0]) makes the empty subarray a valid, zero-sum baseline
        current = 0
        for x in nums:
            current = max(x, current + x)
            best = max(best, current)
        return best

    total_sum = sum(arr)
    doubled = arr if k == 1 else arr + arr                                 # 2 copies are enough to capture any wrap-around subarray shape
    best = kadane_max(doubled)
    if k > 2 and total_sum > 0:
        best += (k - 2) * total_sum                                        # extra full copies only ever help if the whole array's sum is positive
    return best % MOD


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(k_concatenation_max_sum([1, -2, 1], 5))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single Kadane's pass over just 2 copies of arr (length 2n), regardless of how large k is.
Space: O(n) for the doubled array.

Any subarray spanning multiple copies of arr can be decomposed into: a suffix of one copy, some number of complete full copies, and a prefix of another copy. The best possible "suffix + prefix" combination (wrapping across exactly one seam) is already found by running Kadane's on 2 concatenated copies. Any additional complete copies beyond that only ever add value when arr's own total sum is positive (adding a non-positive-sum copy could never help), which is exactly why the (k-2)*totalSum term is included only under that condition.

items: Actually constructing or attempting to iterate over k copies of arr, which becomes intractable for large k (up to 10^5), even though only 2 copies are ever truly needed.
Forgetting the totalSum > 0 condition before adding (k-2)*totalSum, which would incorrectly add a negative or zero contribution when extra copies don't actually help.
Initializing Kadane's running/best values to arr[0] instead of 0, which would produce a negative result for all-negative arrays instead of this problem's required floor of 0.

items: Explicitly justify why 2 copies (not k copies) suffice, and why the extra-copies term requires totalSum > 0, since both of these justifications are the crux of why this solution is correct and independent of k's magnitude.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Maximum subarray sum of an array repeated k times" points toward running Kadane's Algorithm on just 2 concatenated copies, then adding a closed-form (k-2)*totalSum adjustment only when the whole array's sum is positive.

items: Why specifically 2 copies, and not 3 or more? 2 copies are sufficient because any subarray spanning more than 2 copies can be decomposed into a suffix of the first, some number of full copies (accounted for separately via the closed-form term), and a prefix of the last; 2 copies alone already capture every possible "wraps across exactly one seam" shape.

How would you handle potential overflow before applying the modulo? Using a 64-bit (long/long long) accumulator for best and the (k-2)*totalSum term prevents overflow before the final modulo is applied, since totalSum * k can be very large.

What if arr itself could be extremely large (not just k)? The core technique is unaffected, since the algorithm's cost depends only on arr's length (via the O(n) Kadane's pass on 2 copies), never on k.

Builds directly on standard Kadane's Algorithm, combined with the "closed-form extra copies" trick reusable whenever a problem describes a huge, exactly-repeating structure that would be intractable to construct directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O((n * k) squared) time, O(n * k) space.
Optimized (Kadane's on 2 copies + closed-form extra copies): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Standard Kadane's Algorithm on 2 concatenated copies of arr, plus a closed-form adjustment for additional full copies
Core Idea: Only 2 copies are ever needed to capture wrap-around shapes; extra full copies only help (and are added via simple multiplication) when the array's total sum is positive
Time: O(n), independent of k
Space: O(n), independent of k
Most Important Observation: A huge, exactly-repeating structure can often be reasoned about using just a small, fixed number of copies, with the remainder expressed as simple arithmetic
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Kadane's on 2 copies, plus (k-2)*totalSum if totalSum > 0 and k > 2
